newsitem.title: CHINA: Albright vows U.S. will speak out on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Albright vows U.S. will speak out on Hong Kong.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Tuesday promised that the United States would continue to speak out about Hong Kong now that the former British colony was under Chinese control.

Meanwhile, U.S. officials privately expressed satisfaction that Chinese President Jiang Zemin "said the right things" and set the right tone during his speech on Monday night at the ceremony to hand over Hong Kong to Beijing rule.
As she prepared to leave Hong Kong for Washington, Albright said that "although Hong Kong awoke this morning under a changed flag, America's interest here has not changed."
Even though officials and journalists from other countries were leaving Hong Kong with the festivities over, "the world will be watching closely at everything that happens here," she said.

"We will continue to express our deep and abiding interest in the freedom and well-being of the people of Hong Kong...to seek the kind of close cooperation on law enforcement that has led to the extradition from Hong Kong to the United States of more than five dozen drug traffickers and other fugitives since 1991," Albright said.

"We will continue to encourage an open and law-based investment climate for America's largest overseas business community...to seek routine and regular port visits for U.S. navy vessels and will continue to engage Hong Kong in a vigorous programme of social, cultural and academic exchanges," she said.
Albright added: "For China the question is whether it matches its understandable pride at Hong Kong's return with faithful implementation of commitments to maintain its autonomy and way of life."
She spoke at the rededication of the newly-renovated U.S. consulate in Hong Kong.

Separately, a senior U.S. official said he was encouraged that Jiang in his speech "said a number of things about democracy and preserving the way of life (in Hong Kong) that one would have wanted to hear".

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Jiang's tone was serious and he "recognized that the international community is going to have an ongoing interest here and they accept the role the international community is going to continue to play in Hong Kong".
Overall, the speech was positive, the official said.
Although Jiang added the qualifier "basically" when referring to China's commitment to Hong Kong's laws, the U.S. official was not concerned.
"There's no reason to expect that he would say 100 percent of the laws would remain unchanged. In fact on the essentials, he reiterated them."

The official cautioned that "again, we'll see what happens in fact. But given that he began by both referencing democracy -- which was an important thing for him to say -- and talked about maintaining commitments, those were the most important things."
